18-1

Lecture 18-1

Why let the catalyst float?

Limits of a fixed bedFluidizationWhat is gainedWhat it costs

Lecture 18-1

A floating bed solves three fixed-bed problems and creates new ones

  1. Where the fixed bed stopshot spots, pressure drop of fine particles, short catalyst life
  2. What fluidization isgas drag carries the particles; the bed behaves like a liquid
  3. What is gaineduniform temperature, high heat transfer, easy solids handling
  4. What it costsbypassing, backmixing, entrainment, hard scale-up

Lectures 15 to 17 · three limits

Three problems that a bed of resting pellets cannot solve

Hot spots

Pellets do not move, so heat leaves only through the gas and the wall. Strong exotherms make a hot spot.

Lecture 15

Fine particles

Small particles remove pore-diffusion limits, but Ergun pressure drop rises steeply as the particle shrinks.

Lecture 15

Short catalyst life

A catalyst that cokes in seconds to minutes cannot wait for a shutdown, or even for a slow moving bed.

Lecture 17

One idea answers all three: let the gas carry the particles.

Fluidization

When gas drag equals the weight of the particles, the bed floats

  • Low gas velocity: a packed bed; the gas only percolates.
  • At the minimum fluidization velocity the particles separate and the bed flows like a liquid.
  • Extra gas rises as bubbles; the bed looks like a boiling liquid.

Interactive 1 · try it

The same exothermic reaction: a peak in the fixed bed, a flat line in the fluidized bed

fixed-bed peak (°C)–
fluidized bed (°C)–

Illustrative model: first-order reaction, feed and coolant at 327 °C, activation energy 100 kJ/mol.

Moving solids carry heat through the whole bed, so a fluidized bed stays within a few kelvin where a fixed bed runs away.

Advantages

Four gains, all from particles that move

Uniform temperature

Intense solids mixing: no hot spot, even for strongly exothermic reactions.

High heat transfer

Particles wash the cooling tubes, so little tube area removes a large heat duty.

Small particles

Particles of 50–100 µm: large external area, short pores, low pressure drop.

Liquid-like solids

Catalyst is added, withdrawn and sent to a regenerator through pipes, without stopping.

After Werther, Fluidized-Bed Reactors, Ullmann’s Encyclopedia (2012), Section 1.3.

The same motion that mixes the heat also mixes and bypasses the gas.

Disadvantages

Four costs that the rest of this lecture must manage

Gas bypassing

Bubbles carry gas past the catalyst; conversion can fall below mixed flow. Sections 18-5, 18-6.

Backmixing

Mixed solids drag gas down with them: lower conversion and selectivity than plug flow.

Entrainment and attrition

Fine catalyst leaves with the gas and breaks; cyclones are essential. Section 18-7.

Difficult scale-up

A large bed does not behave like a small one. Section 18-9.

No reactor wins every row: a fluidized bed trades contacting quality for temperature control and solids handling.

Section 18-1 · summary

Fluidize when heat, particle size or catalyst life defeats a fixed bed

  • A bed floats when gas drag carries the weight of the particles.
  • Gains: uniform temperature, high heat transfer, fine particles, liquid-like solids.
  • Costs: bypassing, backmixing, entrainment and attrition, difficult scale-up.
  • The choice is a trade between temperature control and contacting quality.

Interactive 1 · catalytic processes

Five processes, five reasons to fluidize

–

–

Process data from Werther, Ullmann’s Encyclopedia (2012), Section 8: the bed type follows the heat load and the catalyst life.

Fluidization is not only for catalysts: sometimes the solid is the product or the fuel.

Beyond catalysis

When the particle itself is the product or the reactant

  • Gas-phase polyethylene: the growing polymer granule is the bed; recycle gas removes the heat.
  • Combustion and gasification: coal or biomass burns in a hot bed of sand or ash.
  • Roasting and calcination: ore particles react with the gas at uniform temperature.
  • Drying and coating: no reaction, the same contacting.

Interactive 2 · particle size and gas velocity

Fine catalysts at low velocity, coarse solids or risers at high velocity

$d_p$ (µm)–
$u_0$ (m/s)–

Typical orders of magnitude: catalytic beds use 50–100 µm powder; velocity then decides bubbling bed or riser.

Three reasons

Ask which of the three a process is paying for

1 · Heat

Strong exotherm or narrow temperature window.

acrylonitrile, maleic anhydride, Fischer–Tropsch, polyethylene

2 · Regeneration

Catalyst dies in seconds to minutes and must circulate to a regenerator.

catalytic cracking, maleic anhydride riser

3 · The solid itself

The particle is the product or the fuel and must be fed and withdrawn continuously.

polyethylene, combustion, roasting

Also (Werther): reactants fed separately allow operation inside the explosion range.

Section 18-2 · summary

Heat, regeneration or solids handling: one of them pays for the fluidized bed

  • Lifetime of seconds: riser with regenerator (catalytic cracking).
  • Strong exotherm: bubbling or turbulent bed with cooling tubes (acrylonitrile).
  • Solid product or fuel: the bed is the process (polyethylene, combustion).
  • Catalytic beds use 50–100 µm powder; velocity sets the regime.

18-3

Lecture 18-3

When does a bed of particles start to float?

Pressure dropMinimum fluidizationTerminal velocityGeldart groups

Lecture 18-3

Two velocities bound the bed, and the powder decides how it behaves between them

  1. Pressure drop against velocitythe curve that shows the bed lifting
  2. Minimum fluidization velocitydrag equals weight: Ergun gives the velocity
  3. Terminal velocitywhere a single particle is blown out
  4. Geldart classificationsize and density predict the bubbling behaviour

The powder

A fluidizable catalyst is a fine, free-flowing powder of microspheres

  • Spray-dried microspheres, typically 50–100 µm, with a spread of sizes.
  • Aerated, the powder pours and levels like a liquid.
  • Hard and round, to resist attrition in cyclones and jets.
  • A share of fines below 44 µm keeps the bubbles small (Section 18-9).

Interactive 1 · the fluidization curve

Pressure drop rises as in a fixed bed, then stays at the weight of the bed

$u_{mf}$ (m/s)–
$u_t$ (m/s)–
$u_t/u_{mf}$–
bed $\Delta P$ (kPa)–

Gas of Example 18.1; bed 1 m deep at minimum fluidization, voidage 0.5.

Above $u_{mf}$ the pressure drop no longer rises with velocity: the gas only has to carry the weight of the bed.

To predict where the curve bends we need five quantities.

Symbols

The quantities that set the two velocity limits

$u_0$
superficial gas velocity: volume flow over empty-vessel area
m/s
$u_{mf}$
minimum fluidization velocity: $u_0$ at which the bed just floats
m/s
$\varepsilon_{mf}$
bed voidage at minimum fluidization, about 0.4–0.5
–
$u_t$
terminal velocity: fall speed of one particle in still gas
m/s
$Ar$
Archimedes number, $d_p^3\rho_g(\rho_s-\rho_g)g/\mu^2$: weight against viscous force
–

$d_p$, $\rho_s$, $\rho_g$, $\mu$: particle diameter and density, gas density and viscosity, as in Lecture 15.

Minimum fluidization step 1 of 2

At $u_{mf}$ the pressure drop carries the buoyant weight of the particles

Ergun, Lecture 15$\dfrac{\Delta P}{H}=\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3}\dfrac{\mu u_0}{d_p^2}+\dfrac{1.75(1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3}\dfrac{\rho_gu_0^2}{d_p}$
$\Delta P\,A=H_{mf}A\,(1-\varepsilon_{mf})(\rho_s-\rho_g)\,g$
drag force equals weight minus buoyancy
$\dfrac{\Delta P}{H_{mf}}=(1-\varepsilon_{mf})(\rho_s-\rho_g)\,g$
divide by area and bed height
Ergun at $u_0=u_{mf}$, $\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{mf}$  =  $(1-\varepsilon_{mf})(\rho_s-\rho_g)\,g$
both hold at the bend of the curve

$H_{mf}$ is the bed height at minimum fluidization (m); $A$ is the bed cross-section (m²).

Minimum fluidization step 2 of 2

In dimensionless form one equation gives $u_{mf}$ for any powder

$\dfrac{1.75}{\varepsilon_{mf}^3}Re_{mf}^2+\dfrac{150(1-\varepsilon_{mf})}{\varepsilon_{mf}^3}Re_{mf}=Ar$
multiply by $d_p^3\rho_g/\mu^2$
$Re_{mf}=\sqrt{33.7^2+0.0408\,Ar}-33.7$
Wen and Yu: typical $\varepsilon_{mf}$ built in
$u_{mf}\approx\dfrac{d_p^2(\rho_s-\rho_g)\,g}{1650\,\mu}$   for $Ar<10^3$
fine particles: viscous term only
$Re_{mf}$
particle Reynolds number at minimum fluidization, $d_p\rho_gu_{mf}/\mu$
–

Fine powders: $u_{mf}\propto d_p^2$. Measure $u_{mf}$ when possible; correlations carry about ±30 %.

The lower limit is $u_{mf}$; the upper reference is the fall speed of one particle.

Terminal velocity

A single particle is carried away when the gas exceeds $u_t$

$d_p^*=Ar^{1/3}$
dimensionless particle size
$u_t^*=\Big[\dfrac{18}{(d_p^*)^2}+\dfrac{0.591}{(d_p^*)^{1/2}}\Big]^{-1}$
Haider and Levenspiel, spheres
$u_t=u_t^*\Big[\dfrac{\mu(\rho_s-\rho_g)\,g}{\rho_g^2}\Big]^{1/3}$
back to m/s

Beds of fine catalyst run well above $u_t$; cyclones return the carry-over (Levenspiel, Ch. 20).

Example 18.1 · problem statement · read first

EXAMPLE 18.1The velocity window of a cracking-type catalyst

A spray-dried catalyst consists of spherical particles with mean diameter 70 µm and particle density 1500 kg/m³. It is fluidized by a hot process gas with density 1.0 kg/m³ and viscosity 3.0 × 10−5 Pa s. The reactor is to operate at a superficial gas velocity of 0.30 m/s.

(a) Calculate the Archimedes number and the minimum fluidization velocity (Wen and Yu).

(b) Calculate the terminal velocity (Haider and Levenspiel).

(c) Compare the operating velocity with both limits. What does the result demand of the hardware?

GivenValue
$d_p$70 µm
$\rho_s$1500 kg/m³
$\rho_g$1.0 kg/m³
$\mu$3.0 × 10−5 Pa s
$u_0$0.30 m/s

Example 18.1 · solution (a)

EXAMPLE 18.1The bed floats at only 1.5 mm/s

Wen and Yu$Ar=\dfrac{d_p^3\rho_g(\rho_s-\rho_g)g}{\mu^2},\qquad Re_{mf}=\sqrt{33.7^2+0.0408\,Ar}-33.7$
$Ar=\dfrac{(70\times10^{-6})^3(1.0)(1499)(9.81)}{(3.0\times10^{-5})^2}=5.60$
SI units throughout
$Re_{mf}=\sqrt{1135.69+0.229}-33.7=3.39\times10^{-3}$
viscous regime, $Ar$ is small
$u_{mf}=\dfrac{Re_{mf}\,\mu}{\rho_gd_p}=\dfrac{3.39\times10^{-3}\times3.0\times10^{-5}}{1.0\times70\times10^{-6}}=1.45\times10^{-3}$ m/s
1.5 mm/s

Example 18.1 · solution (b) and (c)

EXAMPLE 18.1The reactor runs at 200 times $u_{mf}$ and above $u_t$

Haider and Levenspiel$u_t^*=\Big[\dfrac{18}{(d_p^*)^2}+\dfrac{0.591}{(d_p^*)^{1/2}}\Big]^{-1},\quad d_p^*=Ar^{1/3},\quad u_t=u_t^*\Big[\dfrac{\mu(\rho_s-\rho_g)g}{\rho_g^2}\Big]^{1/3}$
$d_p^*=5.60^{1/3}=1.776$;  $u_t^*=\big[5.705+0.443\big]^{-1}=0.163$
Stokes term dominates
$u_t=0.163\times\big[3.0\times10^{-5}\times1499\times9.81\big]^{1/3}=0.163\times0.761=0.124$ m/s
$\rho_g^2=1$
$\dfrac{u_0}{u_{mf}}=\dfrac{0.30}{0.00145}=206$;  $\dfrac{u_0}{u_t}=2.4$
far above both limits

(c) Nearly all gas is excess gas and particles are carried up: freeboard and cyclones are needed.

Two powders with the same $u_{mf}$ can still bubble very differently.

Geldart groups

Particle size and density sort powders into four behaviours

C · cohesive

Below about 20–30 µm. Sticks together; gas channels through. Hard to fluidize.

A · aeratable

About 30–100 µm catalyst. Expands before bubbling; bubbles stay small.

B · sand-like

About 100–1000 µm. Bubbles at $u_{mf}$; bubbles grow large.

D · spoutable

Large or dense. Very large slow bubbles; the bed spouts.

Interactive 2 · classify a powder

Move the powder across the chart and read its group

Geldart group–
$u_{mf}$ in air (m/s)–

Geldart’s boundaries for air at ambient conditions: catalytic reactors aim for group A, where bubbles stay small.

Section 18-3 · summary

Weight sets the pressure drop, $u_{mf}$ the start, the powder group the behaviour

  • Fluidized: $\Delta P/H_{mf}=(1-\varepsilon_{mf})(\rho_s-\rho_g)g$, independent of velocity.
  • $u_{mf}$ from Wen and Yu; for fine powder it scales with $d_p^2$.
  • $u_t$ from Haider and Levenspiel; catalyst beds run above it with cyclones.
  • Geldart A powder (30–100 µm) is the catalyst of choice.

Transition velocities

Three more velocities mark where the regime changes

$u_{mb}=2.07\,e^{0.716F}\,\dfrac{d_p\,\rho_g^{0.06}}{\mu^{0.347}}$
first bubbles, group A (Abrahamsen, Geldart)

Bi and Grace: onset of turbulent fluidization, and of significant entrainment.

A regime of small beds

In a narrow column the bubbles fill the cross-section and become slugs

  • Slugging starts when the bubble reaches about two-thirds of the bed diameter (Knowlton).
  • A slug rises more slowly than a free bubble of the same gas flow.
  • Pilot columns slug; commercial beds do not. This is the trap of Section 18-9.

Section 18-4 · summary

Velocity selects the regime; the regime selects the contacting

  • Order: fixed, bubbling, turbulent, fast fluidization, transport.
  • $u_c$ and $u_{se}$ follow from $Ar$; narrow columns slug instead.
  • Fine catalyst bubbles over a wide window and runs above $u_t$.
  • Above $u_{se}$ the solids must circulate: riser plus return leg.

18-5

Lecture 18-5

What do the bubbles do to the gas?

Two-phase theoryBubble velocityCloud and wakeBubble growth

Lecture 18-5

Most of the gas rides in bubbles that hardly touch the catalyst

  1. Two-phase theoryemulsion stays at minimum fluidization; the rest is bubbles
  2. Bubble velocity and bubble fractionsize alone sets how fast bubbles rise
  3. Cloud and wakewhy bubble gas stays with its bubble
  4. Bubble growthbubbles grow with height until the wall or stability stops them

Two-phase theory

The bed is a dense emulsion plus bubbles almost free of solids

  • The emulsion stays close to minimum fluidization: gas flow $u_{mf}$, voidage $\varepsilon_{mf}$.
  • The excess gas, $u_0-u_{mf}$, rises as bubbles.
  • Example 18.1: $u_0/u_{mf}=206$, so over 99 % of the gas is bubble gas.

Symbols

Five quantities describe the bubble phase

$d_b$
effective bubble diameter: sphere of the same volume
m
$u_{br}$
rise velocity of one bubble in a bed otherwise at $u_{mf}$
m/s
$u_b$
rise velocity of bubbles in a freely bubbling bed
m/s
$\delta$
bubble fraction: bubble volume per bed volume
–
$u_f$
gas velocity between emulsion particles, $u_{mf}/\varepsilon_{mf}$
m/s

Bubble velocity

A bubble rises like a gas bubble in a liquid: its size sets its speed

$u_{br}=0.711\sqrt{g\,d_b}$
Davidson: single bubble, like a spherical cap in liquid
$u_b=u_0-u_{mf}+u_{br}$
bubbles also ride on the excess gas flow
$\delta=\dfrac{u_0}{u_b}$   for fast bubbles
all gas flows through bubbles: $u_0=\delta\,u_b$
$H_f=\dfrac{H_{mf}}{1-\delta}$
bubbles expand the bed above $H_{mf}$

$H_f$ is the height of the bubbling bed (m). Fast bubbles: $u_b>5\,u_f$, true for fine catalyst (Levenspiel, Ch. 20).

A fast bubble does not exchange its gas freely with the emulsion.

Cloud and wake

Gas circulates inside a fast bubble and a thin cloud around it

$\Big(\dfrac{R_c}{R_b}\Big)^3=\dfrac{u_{br}+2u_f}{u_{br}-u_f}$
  • $R_c$, $R_b$: cloud and bubble radius (Davidson).
  • Fast bubble: the cloud is thin, so bubble gas is segregated.
  • Wake solids, fraction $\alpha$ of bubble volume, rise with the bubble and mix the bed.

Interactive 1 · one bubble

Larger bubbles rise faster and keep their gas to themselves

Recall$u_{br}=0.711\sqrt{g\,d_b},\quad u_b=u_0-u_{mf}+u_{br}$
$u_b$ (m/s)–
$\delta$–
$u_b/u_f$–
cloud thickness (% of $d_b$)–
time to cross 3 m (s)–

In fine catalyst the bubble outruns the emulsion gas by a factor of hundreds: the cloud is under 1 % of the bubble size.

Bubble size is the key number, and it is not constant in the bed.

Bubble growth

Bubbles coalesce and grow as they rise

$d_b=\dfrac{0.54\,(u_0-u_{mf})^{0.4}\,\big(z+4\sqrt{A_0}\big)^{0.8}}{g^{0.2}}$
$z$
height above the gas distributor
m
$A_0$
distributor area per orifice; zero for a porous plate
m²
  • Darton correlation, for freely bubbling group B beds.
  • Group A: growth stops at a maximum stable size, about 0.10–0.25 m (Knowlton).
  • Narrow column: growth stops at the wall, as slugs.

Interactive 2 · bubble size against height

What limits the bubble: the powder, or the wall?

$d_b$ at 1 m (m)–
$d_b$ at 3 m (m)–

A 0.3 m pilot column slugs within the first metre; a wide bed of group B powder lets bubbles reach half a metre.

Lectures 11 to 13 · link

The residence time distribution alone cannot predict this reactor

  • Bubble gas passes quickly and meets little catalyst; emulsion gas stays long among much catalyst.
  • So conversion depends on where the gas spends its time, not only how long.
  • Dispersion and tanks-in-series models cannot give conversion below mixed flow, yet bubbling beds do (Levenspiel, Ch. 20).
A model must follow the gas from bubble to cloud to emulsion: Section 18-6.

Section 18-5 · summary

Bubble size sets bubble speed, bubble fraction and bypassing

  • Emulsion at $u_{mf}$; the excess gas rises as bubbles.
  • $u_{br}=0.711\sqrt{g\,d_b}$, $u_b=u_0-u_{mf}+u_{br}$, $\delta=u_0/u_b$.
  • Fast bubbles keep their gas inside a thin cloud; wakes mix the solids.
  • Bubbles grow with height; group A powder and walls limit them.

18-6

Lecture 18-6

How much conversion does a bubbling bed give?

Bubble, cloud, emulsionExchange coefficientsPerformance equationPlug and mixed flow

Lecture 18-6

The Kunii–Levenspiel model turns one bubble size into a conversion

  1. Three regionsgas goes from bubble to cloud to emulsion
  2. Exchange coefficients and solids fractionshow fast gas transfers, how much catalyst each region holds
  3. Performance equationfive resistances combined for a first-order reaction
  4. Against plug flow and mixed flowwhat bypassing costs in catalyst

The K-L model

Reactant must leave the bubble to find the catalyst

  • All bubbles have one size $d_b$ and rise in plug flow.
  • Emulsion stays at $u_{mf}$; its gas is treated as stagnant.
  • Gas enters and leaves only through the bubbles.
  • Given $d_b$, the model predicts everything else (Kunii and Levenspiel).

Symbols

Two exchange coefficients and three solids fractions

$K_{bc}$
gas interchange between bubble and cloud, per bubble volume
s−1
$K_{ce}$
gas interchange between cloud and emulsion, per bubble volume
s−1
$f_b,f_c,f_e$
volume of solids in bubbles, in cloud and wake, in emulsion, per bed volume
–
$k'''$
first-order rate constant per volume of catalyst solid
s−1
$\mathscr{D}$
diffusivity of the reactant in the gas
m²/s

Exchange coefficients

Small bubbles exchange gas quickly; large bubbles hardly at all

$K_{bc}=4.5\,\dfrac{u_{mf}}{d_b}+5.85\,\dfrac{\mathscr{D}^{1/2}g^{1/4}}{d_b^{5/4}}$
through-flow plus diffusion (Davidson)
$K_{ce}=6.77\Big(\dfrac{\varepsilon_{mf}\,\mathscr{D}\,u_{br}}{d_b^{3}}\Big)^{1/2}$
unsteady diffusion at the cloud surface (Higbie)
Lecture 18-5$u_{br}=0.711\sqrt{g\,d_b},\qquad u_b=u_0-u_{mf}+u_{br},\qquad \delta=\dfrac{u_0}{u_b}$

Both coefficients fall steeply with $d_b$: doubling the bubble cuts the exchange to less than half.

Solids fractions

Where the catalyst sits: almost none of it is in the bubbles

$f_b\approx0.001$ to $0.01$
measured: bubbles are nearly empty
$f_c=\delta(1-\varepsilon_{mf})\Big[\dfrac{3u_f}{u_{br}-u_f}+\alpha\Big]$
cloud volume plus wake volume
$f_e=(1-\varepsilon_{mf})(1-\delta)-f_c-f_b$
the rest of the solids
$\alpha$
wake volume per bubble volume; 0.2–2.0 in different studies, 0.33 used here
–

$u_f=u_{mf}/\varepsilon_{mf}$. Equations from Levenspiel, Ch. 20, after Kunii and Levenspiel (1991).

Now write a reactant balance for each region of a thin slice of bed.

Performance equation step 1 of 2

Three balances for a first-order reaction

$-u_0\dfrac{dC_b}{dz}=f_bk'''C_b+\delta K_{bc}(C_b-C_c)$
bubble: plug flow, reaction, loss to cloud
$\delta K_{bc}(C_b-C_c)=f_ck'''C_c+\delta K_{ce}(C_c-C_e)$
cloud: no through-flow
$\delta K_{ce}(C_c-C_e)=f_ek'''C_e$
emulsion: what arrives reacts

$C_b$, $C_c$, $C_e$: reactant concentration in bubble, cloud and emulsion gas (mol/m³). Rates are per unit bed volume.

Performance equation step 2 of 2

Five resistances, in series and parallel, give one rate coefficient

$-u_0\dfrac{dC_b}{dz}=K_f\,C_b$
eliminate $C_e$, then $C_c$
$K_f=f_bk'''+\cfrac{1}{\cfrac{1}{\delta K_{bc}}+\cfrac{1}{f_ck'''+\cfrac{1}{\cfrac{1}{\delta K_{ce}}+\cfrac{1}{f_ek'''}}}}$
$\ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=\dfrac{K_f\,H_f}{u_0}$,   $X_A=1-e^{-K_fH_f/u_0}$
integrate from grid to bed surface

Valid for fast bubbles ($u_b>5u_f$) without slugging. $K_f$ is the overall rate coefficient per bed volume (s−1).

Reading the equation

Plug flow at one end, transfer control at the other

Previous slide$\ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=\dfrac{K_fH_f}{u_0}$
$K_{bc},K_{ce}\to\infty$:  $K_f\to(f_b+f_c+f_e)k'''$,  $\ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=k'''\tau'''$
tiny bubbles: plug flow
$k'''\to\infty$:  $K_f\to f_bk'''+\delta K_{bc}$
fast reaction: bubble-to-cloud transfer controls
$\tau'''$
catalyst volume over gas volume flow, $H_{mf}(1-\varepsilon_{mf})/u_0$
s

$k'''\tau'''$ is the same dimensionless group used for the packed bed in Lecture 5.

Multiple reactions

For A → R → S, bypassing and starved solids cut the yield of R

  • Solids in the emulsion see a much lower reactant concentration than the outlet gas: product R stays there and reacts on to S.
  • The larger the bubbles, the lower the maximum yield of the intermediate, and the more catalyst is needed to reach it (Levenspiel, Ch. 20).
  • So selective oxidations want small bubbles, or a riser.
In Levenspiel’s Example 20.1 the gas leaves at 68 % of the feed concentration while the solids see only about 11 %.

Section 18-6 · summary

One bubble size predicts the conversion, and warns when it will be poor

  • Gas passes bubble → cloud → emulsion; $K_{bc}$ and $K_{ce}$ fall steeply with $d_b$.
  • $\ln(C_{A0}/C_A)=K_fH_f/u_0$: plug flow with $K_f$ replacing $k'''$.
  • Example 18.2: 78 % against 99.5 % in plug flow and 84 % in mixed flow.
  • Fast and selective reactions need small bubbles.

Only the bed converts reactant; every other part exists to feed it, cool it or keep its catalyst.

Heat transfer

Moving particles carry heat to the tube wall far better than gas alone

  • Packets of particles touch the tube, give up heat, and are replaced within a fraction of a second.
  • Typical bed-to-tube coefficient: 200–600 W/m²K, several times a gas-swept fixed-bed wall.
  • The bed is at one temperature, so every tube works with the full driving force.
$Q=h\,A_t\,(T_{bed}-T_{c})$

$A_t$

m²
$T_c$
coolant temperature
K

Catalyst of Example 18.2 at 0.30 m/s: a low-pressure-drop grid lets the gas choose its own path, and part of the bed stays unfluidized.

Keeping the catalyst in

Bursting bubbles throw catalyst upward; the freeboard and cyclones bring it back

  • The solids flux falls with height up to the transport disengaging height (TDH); above it only fine particles remain.
  • Cyclone inlets go above the TDH, usually in two stages.
  • The dipleg returns the catalyst, sealed in the bed or by a flap valve.
  • Reaction continues in the hot freeboard and can lower selectivity (Werther).

Attrition

Catalyst breaks in three places, and the fines it loses matter

Grid jets

High-velocity gas jets at the orifices throw particles against each other.

Bubbling bed

Bubble motion rubs particles together throughout the bed.

Cyclones

Particles hit the cyclone wall at inlet velocity on every pass.

Sources as modelled by Werther (2012). Make-up catalyst replaces lost fines, which also control bubble size.

Section 18-7 · summary

Tubes, grid, freeboard and cyclones make the bed a reactor

  • $Q=hA_t(T_{bed}-T_c)$ with $h$ of 200–600 W/m²K: small tube bundles.
  • Grid pressure drop of 0.2–0.4 of the bed pressure drop.
  • Cyclones above the TDH return the entrained catalyst through diplegs.
  • Attrition at jets, bubbles and cyclones sets the catalyst make-up.

What changes when the solids circulate?

Circulating loopRiser hydrodynamicsRiser modelCatalytic cracking

Lecture 18-8

Above the transport velocity the bed becomes a loop, and the gas returns to near plug flow

  1. The circulating loopriser, cyclone, standpipe and valve
  2. Riser hydrodynamicssolids flux, slip and how little catalyst the riser holds
  3. Riser reactor modelplug flow with a catalyst that decays on the way up
  4. Catalytic crackingriser and regenerator as one heat-balanced unit

Circulating fluidized bed

Solids carried out at the top must come back at the bottom

  • Riser: gas and solids flow upward together at several m/s.
  • Cyclone: separates the solids from the product gas.
  • Standpipe: a dense column whose weight pushes solids back in.
  • Valve: sets the circulation rate, independently of the gas flow.

Symbols

The riser has one more independent variable: the solids flux

Riser hydrodynamics

Solids flux and slip fix how much catalyst the riser holds

$G_s=\rho_s\,\varepsilon_s\,u_p$

  • Lean core moving up, dense annulus sliding down the wall.
  • A denser acceleration zone at the bottom; $\psi\approx2$ holds above it.

$k'''$ = 25 s−1, $u_0$ = 12 m/s, $\psi$ = 2: illustrative values for a very active catalyst.

When coke kills the catalyst in seconds, conversion is bought with more circulation, not more height.

Catalytic cracking

Two fluidized beds in one loop: one cracks, the other burns the coke

  • Riser: hot catalyst vaporizes and cracks the oil in a few seconds, at 480–540 °C.
  • Stripper: steam removes hydrocarbons from the spent catalyst.
  • Regenerator: air burns the coke in a dense bed; the hot catalyst carries that heat back.
  • Classic regenerators ran at 570–590 °C (Werther); modern ones run hotter, near 700 °C.

Section 18-8 · summary

The riser trades catalyst holdup for plug flow and a controllable contact time

  • Loop: riser, cyclone, standpipe, valve; circulation set by the valve.
  • $\varepsilon_s=\psi G_s/(\rho_su_0)$: a few percent, against 35 % in a bubbling bed.
  • Gas near plug flow; conversion ceiling $k'''G_s/(\rho_su_0k_d)$.
  • Cracking: riser for seconds of contact, regenerator for coke and heat.

Lecture 18-9

A large bed is a different reactor, unless the bubbles are kept the same

  1. Why scale-up failsthe slugging pilot and the bubbling plant
  2. What changes with sizebubbles, grid, fines, feed points, freeboard
  3. Controlling bubblespowder, internals and regime

Brownsville, Texas, 1950

A pilot plant that slugged promised yields the full-size reactors never reached

  • Two 5 m bubbling-bed Fischer–Tropsch reactors were built from a 0.3 m pilot plant with group B iron catalyst.
  • The pilot bed slugged: slow slugs gave the gas a long contact time.
  • The large beds bubbled freely: large, fast bubbles, short contact, and far lower yield.

Knowlton (2013), after Squires (1982). The plant made engineers wary of fluidized beds for years.

A narrow pilot column flatters the reactor; group A powder or baffles freeze the bubble size so the plant behaves like the pilot.

What changes with size

Five things differ between the laboratory bed and the plant

FactorLaboratoryPlantEffect on conversion
Bed diameterwalls hold bubbles backbubbles rise fasterlower
Gas distributorporous platenozzles or orificeslower
Fines in the catalystas loadedlost unless cyclones keep themlower if lost
Feed distributionuniform by sizeseparate feed pointsuneven
Freeboardcooled by the wallhot, with much solidextra reaction, lower selectivity

After Werther, Ullmann’s Encyclopedia (2012), Section 10.

Every item on that list acts through bubble size, so control the bubbles.

Controlling bubbles

Three ways to keep bubbles small at any scale

Powder

Group A catalyst with 30–40 % fines below 44 µm: bubbles split at a small stable size.

Werther

Internals

Tube bundles and horizontal baffles break bubbles and limit backmixing of the gas.

Werther; Knowlton

Regime

Turbulent beds have short-lived voids of similar size in small and large vessels.

Knowlton

Sasol replaced 16 circulating reactors by 8 turbulent beds of 10.7 m diameter (Section 18-2).

From laboratory to plant

Each scale answers a different question

Bench and pilot diameters from Werther (2012): a 450–600 mm pilot should allow reliable scale-up.

catalyst/oil–
circulation, 200 t/h feed (t/min)–

More coke heats the regenerator, which cuts the circulation, the conversion and then the coke: the unit balances itself.

Section 18-9 · summary

Scale the bubbles, not only the vessel

  • Narrow pilots slug and overstate conversion; wide beds bubble freely.
  • Diameter, grid, fines, feed points and freeboard all change with size.
  • Control bubbles with group A powder, fines, internals or the turbulent regime.
  • Bench for kinetics, cold model for flow, 0.5 m pilot for both together.

Problem 18.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 18.1Velocity window of a sand-like catalyst

A cold-flow model is to be run with air at ambient conditions (density 1.2 kg/m³, viscosity 1.8 × 10−5 Pa s) and a catalyst carrier of spherical particles, diameter 250 µm and particle density 2500 kg/m³.

(a) Calculate the Archimedes number and the minimum fluidization velocity. (b) Calculate the terminal velocity. (c) Find the Geldart group. (d) Estimate the velocity at which the bed becomes turbulent, and name the regime at $u_0$ = 0.50 m/s.

GivenValue
$d_p$250 µm
$\rho_s$2500 kg/m³
$\rho_g$1.2 kg/m³
$\mu$1.8 × 10−5 Pa s
$u_0$0.50 m/s

Problem 18.1 · solution

PROBLEM 18.1Group B: fluidizes at 0.051 m/s and bubbles up to about 1.9 m/s

Lectures 18-3, 18-4$Re_{mf}=\sqrt{33.7^2+0.0408Ar}-33.7,\quad u_t^*=\Big[\dfrac{18}{(d_p^*)^2}+\dfrac{0.591}{(d_p^*)^{1/2}}\Big]^{-1},\quad Re_c=1.24Ar^{0.45}$
(a) $Ar=1419$;  $Re_{mf}=\sqrt{1193.6}-33.7=0.848$;  $u_{mf}=0.051$ m/s
$u=Re\,\mu/(\rho_gd_p)$
(b) $d_p^*=11.24$;  $u_t^*=[0.143+0.176]^{-1}=3.14$;  $u_t=3.14\times0.674=2.11$ m/s
scale $[\mu(\rho_s-\rho_g)g/\rho_g^2]^{1/3}$
(c) $2.5\times250=625>225$ and $2.5\times250^2=1.6\times10^5<10^6$: group B
g/cm³ and µm
(d) $Re_c=1.24\times1419^{0.45}=32.5$;  $u_c=1.95$ m/s. At 0.50 m/s: bubbling, $u_0/u_{mf}=9.8$
below $u_c$ and below $u_t$

Problem 18.2 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 18.2Bubbles in that bed

The bed of Problem 18.1 ($u_{mf}$ = 0.051 m/s, $\varepsilon_{mf}$ = 0.50) is fluidized at $u_0$ = 0.50 m/s above a perforated plate for which $4\sqrt{A_0}$ = 0.03 m.

(a) Estimate the bubble diameter 1.0 m above the plate with the Darton correlation.

(b) Calculate the bubble rise velocity and the bubble fraction at that height.

(c) Is the bubble fast? Estimate the cloud thickness as a fraction of the bubble diameter.

(d) The cold-flow column is 0.30 m in diameter. What will be observed at this height?

Problem 18.2 · solution

PROBLEM 18.2A free bubble would be 0.25 m, so the 0.30 m column slugs

Lecture 18-5$d_b=\dfrac{0.54(u_0-u_{mf})^{0.4}(z+4\sqrt{A_0})^{0.8}}{g^{0.2}},\quad u_{br}=0.711\sqrt{gd_b},\quad \Big(\dfrac{R_c}{R_b}\Big)^3=\dfrac{u_{br}+2u_f}{u_{br}-u_f}$
(a) $d_b=\dfrac{0.54\,(0.449)^{0.4}(1.03)^{0.8}}{9.81^{0.2}}=\dfrac{0.54\times0.726\times1.024}{1.579}=0.254$ m
excess velocity 0.449 m/s
(b) $u_{br}=1.12$ m/s;  $u_b=0.449+1.12=1.57$ m/s;  $\delta=\dfrac{0.50}{1.57}=0.32$
fast-bubble form of $\delta$
(c) $u_f=0.102$ m/s; $u_b/u_f=15$: fast. $\dfrac{R_c}{R_b}=\Big(\dfrac{1.327}{1.021}\Big)^{1/3}=1.09$: cloud about 5 % of $d_b$
thicker than in fine catalyst
(d) $\tfrac{2}{3}\times0.30=0.20$ m $<0.254$ m: slugging
Section 18-4

Problem 18.3 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 18.3Conversion in a bubbling bed

A first-order reaction A → R runs in a bubbling bed 3.0 m in diameter holding 15 t of group A catalyst (particle density 1500 kg/m³). Data: $u_0$ = 0.25 m/s, $u_{mf}$ = 0.0015 m/s, $\varepsilon_{mf}$ = 0.50, $\alpha$ = 0.33, diffusivity 2.0 × 10−5 m²/s, $f_b$ = 0.001, $k'''$ = 0.80 s−1, effective bubble diameter 0.08 m.

(a) Calculate $u_b$, $\delta$, $H_{mf}$ and $H_f$.

(b) Calculate $K_{bc}$, $K_{ce}$, $f_c$, $f_e$ and $K_f$.

(c) Calculate the conversion and compare it with plug flow and mixed flow.

GivenValue
Bed diameter3.0 m
Catalyst15 t
$u_0$0.25 m/s
$d_b$0.08 m
$k'''$0.80 s−1
$u_{mf}$, $\varepsilon_{mf}$0.0015 m/s, 0.50

Problem 18.3 · solution

PROBLEM 18.381 % in the bubbling bed, 99 % in plug flow, 82 % in mixed flow

K-L model, Lecture 18-6$K_f=f_bk'''+\Big[\dfrac{1}{\delta K_{bc}}+\Big(f_ck'''+\Big[\dfrac{1}{\delta K_{ce}}+\dfrac{1}{f_ek'''}\Big]^{-1}\Big)^{-1}\Big]^{-1},\qquad \ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=\dfrac{K_fH_f}{u_0}$
(a) $u_{br}=0.630$, $u_b=0.878$ m/s; $\delta=0.285$; $H_{mf}=\dfrac{15\,000}{1500\times7.07\times0.5}=2.83$ m; $H_f=3.96$ m
area 7.07 m²
(b) $K_{bc}=1.17$, $K_{ce}=0.751$ s−1; $f_c=0.049$, $f_e=0.308$; $K_f=0.106$ s−1
$\delta K_{bc}=0.334$, $\delta K_{ce}=0.214$
(c) $\ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=\dfrac{0.106\times3.96}{0.25}=1.68$;  $X_A=0.81$
K-L
$k'''\tau'''=\dfrac{0.80\times2.83\times0.5}{0.25}=4.53$:  $X_{PF}=0.989$, $X_{MF}=0.819$
ideal limits

Problem 18.4 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 18.4Catalyst for 90 % conversion

Problem 18.3: bed 3.0 m in diameter, $u_0$ = 0.25 m/s, $k'''$ = 0.80 s−1, $u_{mf}$ = 0.0015 m/s, $\varepsilon_{mf}$ = 0.50; with $d_b$ = 0.08 m: $\delta$ = 0.285, $K_f$ = 0.106 s−1.

The reactor of Problem 18.3 must reach 90 % conversion at the same gas flow.

(a) How much catalyst is needed if the bubbles stay at 0.08 m?

(b) Repeat for bubbles of 0.05 m ($\delta$ = 0.335, $K_f$ = 0.153 s−1) and 0.15 m ($\delta$ = 0.225, $K_f$ = 0.0529 s−1).

(c) Compare with a plug-flow reactor. What do you conclude about bed internals?

$d_b$ (m)$\delta$$K_f$ (s−1)
0.050.3350.153
0.080.2850.106
0.150.2250.0529

Problem 18.4 · solution

PROBLEM 18.413 t, 21 t or 45 t: the bubble size sets the reactor size

K-L, rearranged$H_{mf}=\dfrac{(1-\delta)\,u_0}{K_f}\ln\dfrac{1}{1-X_A},\qquad W=\rho_s\,A\,(1-\varepsilon_{mf})\,H_{mf}$
(a) $H_{mf}=\dfrac{0.715\times0.25}{0.106}\times2.303=3.89$ m;  $W=1500\times7.07\times0.5\times3.89=20.6$ t
$H_f=H_{mf}/(1-\delta)$ substituted
(b) 0.05 m: $H_{mf}=2.51$ m, $W=13.3$ t.  0.15 m: $H_{mf}=8.44$ m, $W=44.7$ t
same formula
(c) Plug flow: $H_{mf}=\dfrac{2.303\times0.25}{0.80\times0.5}=1.44$ m, $W=7.6$ t
$k'''\tau'''=\ln 10$

Tripling the bubble size more than triples the catalyst: internals pay for themselves.

Problem 18.5 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 18.5From a slugging pilot to a 5 m reactor

A first-order reaction ($k'''$ = 0.80 s−1) was tested in a pilot bed 0.30 m in diameter with a group B catalyst: $u_{mf}$ = 0.030 m/s, $\varepsilon_{mf}$ = 0.50, $u_0$ = 0.30 m/s, $H_{mf}$ = 3.0 m. The pilot bed slugged. A commercial bed 5.0 m in diameter is planned with the same $u_0$ and $H_{mf}$. Use $\alpha$ = 0.33, diffusivity 2.0 × 10−5 m²/s, $f_b$ = 0.001 and $4\sqrt{A_0}$ = 0.03 m.

(a) Compare the rise velocity of slugs in the pilot, $u_0-u_{mf}+0.35\sqrt{gD}$, with that of bubbles at mid-height (1.5 m) in the commercial bed.

(b) Estimate the commercial conversion with the K-L model at the mid-height bubble size.

(c) Baffles limit the bubbles to 0.10 m. Estimate the conversion again.

Problem 18.5 · solution

PROBLEM 18.5Free bubbles rise 70 % faster than slugs and convert only 45 %; baffles restore 86 %

Lectures 18-5, 18-6$d_b=\dfrac{0.54(u_0-u_{mf})^{0.4}(z+4\sqrt{A_0})^{0.8}}{g^{0.2}},\quad u_b=u_0-u_{mf}+0.711\sqrt{gd_b},\quad \ln\dfrac{C_{A0}}{C_A}=\dfrac{K_fH_f}{u_0}$
(a) Slugs: $0.27+0.35\sqrt{9.81\times0.30}=0.87$ m/s
pilot column
Bubbles: $d_b=0.285$ m;  $u_b=0.27+0.711\sqrt{9.81\times0.285}=1.46$ m/s
Darton at $z=1.5$ m
(b) $\delta=0.206$, $H_f=3.78$ m, $K_f=0.0472$ s−1:  $X_A=0.45$
$\delta K_{bc}=0.143$, $\delta K_{ce}=0.032$
(c) $d_b=0.10$ m: $\delta=0.308$, $H_f=4.33$ m, $K_f=0.136$ s−1:  $X_A=0.86$
same equations

Plug flow gives 98 % ($k'''\tau'''=4.0$). A pilot result transfers only if its bubble size does.

Class Activity

How to work these problems

  • Start every problem with $Ar$, $u_{mf}$ and the Geldart group: they decide which equations apply.
  • Check the fast-bubble condition before using the K-L equation.
  • State the bubble size you assumed: it is the most uncertain number in the answer.
  • Compare with plug flow and mixed flow to see what bypassing costs.

Lecture 18

Key Takeaways

1

Choose a fluidized bed for strong heat effects, fine or short-lived catalyst, or solids that must flow.

2

Find $Ar$, $u_{mf}$, $u_t$ and the Geldart group first; they fix the velocity window and the bubbling behaviour.

3

Predict conversion with K-L: $\ln(C_{A0}/C_A)=K_fH_f/u_0$, and expect it below mixed flow when bubbles are large.

4

Design the hardware around the bed: tubes for heat, a grid with 0.2–0.4 of the bed pressure drop, cyclones above the TDH.

5

Scale the bubbles: group A powder, fines, internals or a turbulent bed; use a riser when the catalyst lives seconds.
